## A Bad Morning {.center}

> "The portfolio was diversified. Low correlations everywhere."
>
> Then one shock arrived — and everything fell at once.

. . .

**What did the number miss?**

That question drives this entire lecture.

## Your Data

In finance you work with:

- **Daily returns** — fat-tailed, volatility-clustered
- **Factor exposures** — linear structure, but the residuals aren't
- **Credit tables** — binary outcomes, group structure

The *joint* behaviour is what matters.  Marginals lie.

## Why It's Hard — The Shapes

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 350
t = rng.normal(size=n)
x1 = 0.8*t + 0.4*rng.normal(size=n); y1 = 0.8*t + 0.4*rng.normal(size=n)  # linear
x2 = rng.uniform(-2.5,2.5,n); y2 = x2**2 + 0.5*rng.normal(size=n)          # U-shape
x3 = rng.normal(size=n); y3 = rng.normal(size=n)                             # tail crash
crash = rng.random(n) < 0.08
x3[crash] -= rng.uniform(2,4,crash.sum()); y3[crash] -= rng.uniform(2,4,crash.sum())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.8))
titles = ["Linear (Pearson sees this)", "Non-linear (Pearson blind)", "Tail crash (Pearson blind)"]
data = [(x1,y1,COOL,None), (x2,y2,WARM,None), (x3,y3,COOL,crash)]
for ax, (x,y,col,m), title in zip(axes, data, titles):
    if m is None:
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=12, c=col, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
    else:
        ax.scatter(x[~m], y[~m], s=12, c=col, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
        ax.scatter(x[m], y[m], s=20, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## The Running Characters {.center}

We follow **two pairs** down every rung of the ladder.

. . .

**The banks** — strong dependence + joint crashes.
Pearson says "high". The lesson is the extra tail risk it misses.

. . .

**The convex payoff** — $v = |u| + \text{noise}$.
Pearson says "nothing". The ladder's hero case.

## Two Roads to Measure Dependence

There are only **two ways** to ask "how much do these move together?"

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Road 1 — compare directly**

`compare( T(x), T(y) )` — no density needed

- Pearson
- Spearman
- distance correlation
- HSIC / CKA
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
**Road 2 — through the density**

*how far is the joint from independent, in bits?*

- entropy → mutual information
- total correlation
- Linfoot R
- Gaussianization
:::

::::

. . .

The **transform** $T$ is the thread through both.

---

## Two Roads — Same Data, Both Ways

```{python}
#| echo: false
a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=2000)
ra, rb = rankdata(a), rankdata(b)
fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 3.9))
ax0.scatter(a, b, s=8, c=INK, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
ax0.set_title("The data", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
ax1.scatter(ra, rb, s=8, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
ax1.set_title(f"Road 1 · compare transforms\ncorr(rank a, rank b) = {pearsonr(ra, rb)[0]:.2f}",
              fontsize=13)
grid = np.linspace(-4.2, 2.8, 120)
XX, YY = np.meshgrid(grid, grid)
Z = gaussian_kde(np.vstack([a, b]))(np.vstack([XX.ravel(), YY.ravel()])).reshape(XX.shape)
Zind = gaussian_kde(a)(grid)[None, :] * gaussian_kde(b)(grid)[:, None]
ax2.contourf(XX, YY, Z, levels=10, cmap="Oranges")
ax2.contour(XX, YY, Zind, levels=6, colors=COOL, linewidths=1.4)
ax2.set_title(f"Road 2 · through the density\nMI = {mutual_information_xy(a, b) / np.log(2):.2f} bits",
              fontsize=13)
for ax in (ax0, ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Road 1 never touches a density — it reshapes the **points** and compares them.
Road 2 fits the **density** (orange) and measures its gap from the independent
version (blue contours) — in **bits**.

---

## Road 1 · Compare Directly {.center}

No density required — **transform** each variable, then measure a **distance**:

`measure = compare( transform(x), transform(y) )`

. . .

Four rungs of increasing reach:
**Pearson → Spearman → distance correlation → HSIC**.

---

## #1 Pearson — The Line

$$r = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\,\sigma_Y} \in [-1, 1]$$

- Measures **linear** co-movement only
- Fast, familiar, the default everywhere

## #1 Pearson — In Pictures

```{python}
#| echo: false
x, y = datasets.correlated_returns(rho=0.6)
r = np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.scatter(x, y, s=14, alpha=0.5, color=COOL)
plotting.finalize(ax, f"Pearson r = {r:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Asset A return"); ax.set_ylabel("Asset B return")
despine(ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## #1 Pearson — What Noise Does

Same line every panel — only the **scatter around it** grows:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 3.3
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 300
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
eps = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11.5, 3.3))
for ax, s in zip(axes, [0.33, 0.75, 1.33, 2.29]):
    y = x + s * eps
    ax.axline((0, 0), slope=1, color=INK, lw=1.3, ls="--", alpha=0.6)
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=10, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(f"more noise →   r = {pearsonr(x, y)[0]:.2f}", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlim(-3.5, 3.5); ax.set_ylim(-6, 6)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The slope never changed — yet $r$ slides from 0.95 to 0.45. Pearson rates how
**tightly** points hug the line, not whether a link is there: noise alone can make
a real relationship look weak.

The convex pair: Pearson ≈ 0 despite $v$ being almost a deterministic function of $u$.

## #2 Spearman — Ranks

$$\rho_S = \operatorname{corr}(\operatorname{rank}(X),\; \operatorname{rank}(Y))$$

Only one slot changes from Pearson — the **transform**:

```
Pearson   = corr( x       , y       )
Spearman  = corr( rank(x) , rank(y) )
```

Catches any *monotonic* relationship.  Fails on U-shapes.

## #2 Spearman — The Transform, Seen

Take a **compounding payoff** — money that grows multiplicatively, like reinvested
returns or compound interest ($y \approx e^{0.9x}$). Monotonic, but curved:

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 400
x = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
y = np.exp(0.9 * x) * (1 + 0.18 * rng.normal(size=n))   # compounding payoff
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.9))
axL.scatter(x, y, s=12, c=WARM, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title(f"Raw data — compounding payoff\nPearson r = {pearsonr(x, y)[0]:.2f}", fontsize=13)
axR.scatter(rankdata(x), rankdata(y), s=12, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
axR.set_title(f"After the transform — rank(x) vs rank(y)\nPearson on ranks = Spearman = {spearmanr(x, y)[0]:.2f}",
              fontsize=13)
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The bend costs Pearson about a third of its value; **ranks straighten the curve**
— Spearman *is* Pearson on the right panel.

## #2 Spearman — The Seed

Notice: Pearson and Spearman are the **same move**, different transform.

```
general = compare( transform(x) , transform(y) )
```

. . .

**First road**: compare directly, never needing the distribution.

Plant the seed: *do you need the distribution?*
**No** → stay here. **Yes** → the other road.

## Same Correlation, Different Reality

**All four share Pearson ≈ 0.30** — yet each hides a different reality.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
N, TARGET = 600, 0.30

def tune(xx, struct, target, rng):
    s = (struct - struct.mean()) / struct.std()
    ind = rng.normal(0, 1, len(xx)); ind = (ind - ind.mean()) / ind.std()
    best = None
    for w in np.linspace(0.05, 1, 200):
        yy = w * s + (1 - w) * ind
        r = pearsonr(xx, yy)[0]
        if best is None or abs(abs(r) - target) < abs(abs(best[1]) - target):
            best = (yy, r)
    return best

xa = rng.normal(0, 1, N); ya, ra = tune(xa, xa, TARGET, rng)
xb = rng.uniform(-3, 3, N); yb, rb = tune(xb, -(xb**2)+0.9*xb, TARGET, rng)
xc0 = rng.normal(0,1,N); yc0 = rng.normal(0,1,N); rc, crash_c = None, None
for frac in np.linspace(0.04, 0.18, 40):
    m = rng.random(N) < frac
    xx, yy = xc0.copy(), yc0.copy()
    sh = rng.uniform(1.3, 3.2, m.sum())
    xx[m] = -sh + rng.normal(0, .18, m.sum()); yy[m] = -sh + rng.normal(0, .18, m.sum())
    r = pearsonr(xx, yy)[0]
    if rc is None or abs(r - TARGET) < abs(rc - TARGET):
        rc, crash_c, xc, yc = r, m, xx, yy
xd = rng.uniform(-3, 3, N); nd = rng.normal(0, 1, N)
best_d = None
for a in np.linspace(0, 1.3, 220):
    yy = a * xd + nd * (0.25 + 0.7 * np.abs(xd))
    r = pearsonr(xd, yy)[0]
    if best_d is None or abs(r - TARGET) < abs(best_d[1] - TARGET):
        best_d = (yy, r)
yd, rd = best_d

panels = [("Linear", xa, ya, ra, None), ("Curved", xb, yb, rb, None),
          ("Quiet, then crash", xc, yc, rc, crash_c), ("Drift + rising risk", xd, yd, rd, None)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10.5, 6.0))
for ax, (t, x, y, r, mask) in zip(axes.flat, panels):
    if mask is None:
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=22, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
    else:
        ax.scatter(x[~mask], y[~mask], s=22, c=COOL, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none")
        ax.scatter(x[mask], y[mask], s=34, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(f"{t}    ·    Pearson = {r:+.2f}", fontsize=14)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## #3 Distance Correlation — Any Shape

$$\operatorname{dCor}(X, Y) \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{dCov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{dVar}(X)\,\operatorname{dVar}(Y)}} \;\in\; [0, 1]$$

Same template, a new transform — still **no density**:

```
Pearson  = corr(  x       ,  y       )
dCor     = corr(  dist(x) ,  dist(y) )
```

- $\operatorname{dCov}^2 = \overline{A_{ij}\,B_{ij}}$ — average product of the **centered distances**
- **Zero if and only if independent** — any shape counts

---

## #3 Distance Correlation — The Transform

The transform, seen: one day becomes its **distances to every other day**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
def convex_clean(n=120, noise=0.08, seed=42):
    # the convex pair with the noise turned down, so matrix structure is visible
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    u = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    return u, np.abs(u) + noise * rng.normal(0, 1, n)


u, v = convex_clean()
order = np.argsort(u)
us, vs = u[order], v[order]
A = np.abs(us[:, None] - us[None, :])
B = np.abs(vs[:, None] - vs[None, :])
i = 12  # anchor day, low u
fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 3.9))
ax0.scatter(us, vs, s=14, c=WARM, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none")
ax0.scatter([us[i]], [vs[i]], s=70, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
for j in range(0, len(us), 14):
    ax0.plot([us[i], us[j]], [vs[i], vs[j]], color=GRID, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
ax0.set_title("One day vs every other day", fontsize=13)
despine(ax0)
for ax, M, ttl, cmap in [(ax1, A, "all pairwise distances in X", "Blues"),
                         (ax2, B, "all pairwise distances in Y", "Oranges")]:
    ax.imshow(M, cmap=cmap, origin="lower")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=13)
    ax.axhline(i, color=CRASH, lw=1.4)
for ax in (ax0, ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Days sorted by $x$.  The X-distances form a smooth gradient; the Y-distances show
the V as a **cross** — the structure survives the transform, no density in sight.

---

## #3 Distance Correlation — Then Compare

Then the **same move as always** — Pearson, on the *centered distances*:

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 300
u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=n)
xi, yi = rng.normal(size=n), rng.normal(size=n)


def centered_distances(z):
    d = np.abs(z[:, None] - z[None, :])
    return d - d.mean(0) - d.mean(1)[:, None] + d.mean()


sub = rng.choice(n * n, 4000, replace=False)
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.9))
for ax, (x, y), name, col in [(axL, (u, v), "Convex pair", WARM),
                              (axR, (xi, yi), "Independent pair", COOL)]:
    Ac, Bc = centered_distances(x).ravel()[sub], centered_distances(y).ravel()[sub]
    ax.scatter(Ac, Bc, s=6, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\ncorr of centered distances = {pearsonr(Ac, Bc)[0]:.2f}"
                 f"   ·   dCor = {distance_correlation(x, y):.2f}", fontsize=13)
    ax.set_xlabel("centered |xi − xj|", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel("centered |yi − yj|", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

That correlation *is* **dCor²** — dependence of any shape becomes a plain
linear trend in distance space.

---

## From Distance to Kernel

dCor compared days by **distance**. A **kernel** measures the opposite —
**similarity** — by squashing that same distance through a Gaussian:

$$k(x_i, x_j) = \exp\!\Big(\!-\tfrac{|x_i - x_j|^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big) \in (0, 1]$$

. . .

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.5
d = np.linspace(0, 3, 400)
k = np.exp(-d**2 / 2.0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.5))
ax.plot(d, k, color=COOL, lw=3)
ax.fill_between(d, k, color=COOL, alpha=0.08)
ax.scatter([0], [1], s=80, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
ax.annotate("identical days → 1", (0, 1), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(14, -4),
            fontsize=12, color=INK)
df = 2.2
ax.scatter([df], [np.exp(-df**2 / 2)], s=80, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
ax.annotate("far apart → ~0", (df, np.exp(-df**2 / 2)), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(2, 18), fontsize=12, color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("distance  |xᵢ − xⱼ|   (what dCor used)")
ax.set_ylabel("kernel similarity  k")
ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.10)
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

Same ingredient as dCor — the pairwise distance — now read as **nearness**,
bounded to $[0, 1]$.

---

## One Structure, Two Lenses

The pairwise matrix dCor built from **distances** is the one HSIC reads as
**similarity** — top row vs bottom row, same days:

. . .

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.1
from matplotlib.gridspec import GridSpec

def _convex(n=120, noise=0.08, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    u = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    return u, np.abs(u) + noise * rng.normal(0, 1, n)

def _rbf(z):
    d2 = (z[:, None] - z[None, :]) ** 2
    s = np.sqrt(np.median(d2[d2 > 0]) / 2)
    return np.exp(-d2 / (2 * s * s))

uq, vq = _convex(); order = np.argsort(uq); us, vs = uq[order], vq[order]
DX = np.abs(us[:, None] - us[None, :]); DY = np.abs(vs[:, None] - vs[None, :])
KX, KY = _rbf(us), _rbf(vs)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 4.1))
gs = GridSpec(2, 3, width_ratios=[1.15, 1, 1], wspace=0.2, hspace=0.4)
axS = fig.add_subplot(gs[:, 0]); anchor = 12
axS.scatter(us, vs, s=12, c=WARM, alpha=0.45, edgecolors="none")
axS.scatter([us[anchor]], [vs[anchor]], s=70, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
for j in range(0, len(us), 14):
    axS.plot([us[anchor], us[j]], [vs[anchor], vs[j]], color=GRID, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
axS.set_title("one day vs every other", fontsize=12)
axS.set_xticks([]); axS.set_yticks([]); despine(axS)
for spec, M, ttl, cmap in [(gs[0, 1], DX, "distance · X", "Blues"),
                           (gs[0, 2], DY, "distance · Y", "Oranges"),
                           (gs[1, 1], KX, "kernel · X", "Blues"),
                           (gs[1, 2], KY, "kernel · Y", "Oranges")]:
    ax = fig.add_subplot(spec); ax.imshow(M, cmap=cmap, origin="lower")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=12); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

Top: **distance** (dCor); bottom: the **kernel** — the same matrix inverted. HSIC
reads *alike* where dCor read *far*.

---

## #4 HSIC — Dependence Without a Density {.center}

Same template as every rung — a new transform, then **correlate**:

```
Pearson  = corr(  x         ,  y         )
Spearman = corr(  rank(x)   ,  rank(y)   )
dCor     = corr(  dist(x)   ,  dist(y)   )
CKA      = corr(  kernel(x) ,  kernel(y) )
```

. . .

- Zero *exactly* under independence
- No density estimate needed
- **Any kernel** → vectors, sequences, even whole distributions

. . .

CKA is HSIC rescaled to $[0,1]$ — the kernel cousin of dCor.
*The same score becomes the fairness penalty in Lecture 2.*

---

## #4 HSIC — In Pictures

Swap *distance* for **kernel similarity**: $K_{ij}$ = how alike days $i$ and $j$ are.

. . .

```{python}
#| echo: false
u, v = convex_clean()
order = np.argsort(u)
us, vs = u[order], v[order]


def rbf_gram(z):
    d2 = (z[:, None] - z[None, :]) ** 2
    s = np.sqrt(np.median(d2[d2 > 0]) / 2)
    return np.exp(-d2 / (2 * s * s))


K, L = rbf_gram(us), rbf_gram(vs)
nk = len(us)
H = np.eye(nk) - np.ones((nk, nk)) / nk
agree = (H @ K @ H) * (H @ L @ H)
vmax = np.percentile(np.abs(agree), 98)
fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 3.9))
for ax, M, ttl, cmap, kw in [
    (ax0, K, "similar days in X", "Blues", {}),
    (ax1, L, "similar days in Y", "Oranges", {}),
    (ax2, agree, f"where the patterns agree\nCKA = {cka_rbf(u, v):.2f}", "PuOr",
     {"vmin": -vmax, "vmax": vmax}),
]:
    ax.imshow(M, cmap=cmap, origin="lower", **kw)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=13)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

The score just **sums the third panel** — HSIC (and its $[0,1]$ cousin CKA) is
large when the two similarity patterns light up in the same places.

## Road 1 · Side by Side

Same two characters, all four rungs.  Each new rung catches what the last missed:

```{python}

ax.bar(xs + wbar / 2, convex, wbar, color=WARM, label="Convex (a V)")
```

## From Points to a Density

Road 1 compared the **points**. Road 2 steps back to their whole **shape** — the
density $p(x)$ the points trace out:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 2.9
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
pts1d = np.concatenate([rng.normal(0, 1.0, 500), rng.normal(0.5, 2.6, 120)])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 2.9))
axes[0].scatter(pts1d, rng.uniform(0, 1, len(pts1d)), s=9, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
axes[0].set_title("a pile of points", fontsize=13)
axes[1].hist(pts1d, bins=28, color=COOL, alpha=0.75)
axes[1].set_title("count them in bins", fontsize=13)
gx = np.linspace(pts1d.min(), pts1d.max(), 250)
axes[2].fill_between(gx, gaussian_kde(pts1d)(gx), color=COOL, alpha=0.45)
axes[2].plot(gx, gaussian_kde(pts1d)(gx), color=INK, lw=2)
axes[2].set_title("a smooth density  p(x)", fontsize=13)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

Pile up enough days and the cloud becomes a curve. *That curve is what the second
road measures.*

---

## A Distribution's Shape — Its Moments

A density's shape is captured by a few **moments**:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
from scipy.stats import skewnorm
a_sk, loc, sc = 5.0, -1.2, 2.2
gx = np.linspace(-5, 7, 500); pdf = skewnorm.pdf(gx, a_sk, loc, sc)
mu = skewnorm.mean(a_sk, loc, sc); sd = skewnorm.std(a_sk, loc, sc); pk = pdf.max()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.2))
ax.fill_between(gx, pdf, color=COOL, alpha=0.30); ax.plot(gx, pdf, color=INK, lw=2.2)
ax.axvline(mu, color=CRASH, lw=2.2)
ax.annotate("mean", (mu, pk * 0.78), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(7, 0),
            color=CRASH, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
ax.annotate("", xy=(mu + sd, pk * 0.40), xytext=(mu - sd, pk * 0.40),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=INK, lw=1.6))
ax.text(mu, pk * 0.44, "std (spread)", ha="center", fontsize=11, color=INK)
ax.annotate("skew — leans right", xy=(mu + 1.9 * sd, pk * 0.16), xytext=(mu + 1.0 * sd, pk * 0.62),
            fontsize=11, color="#555", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#999", lw=1.2))
ax.annotate("kurtosis — fat tail", xy=(mu + 3.0 * sd, pk * 0.04), xytext=(mu + 1.7 * sd, pk * 0.30),
            fontsize=11, color="#555", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#999", lw=1.2))
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

**mean** (where) · **variance** (how wide) · **skew** (lopsided) · **kurtosis**
(fat tails) — and we never know them exactly, only **estimate** them from a sample.

---

## Two Variables: the Joint and Its Marginals

Two variables have one **joint** shape and two **marginal** shadows:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.0
#| fig-height: 4.3
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
pts = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1.0, 0.72], [0.72, 1.0]], 700)
xx, yy = pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1]
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(xx, yy))
ordr = vals.argsort()[::-1]; vals, vecs = vals[ordr], vecs[:, ordr]
ang = np.degrees(np.arctan2(vecs[1, 0], vecs[0, 0])); ew, eh = 2 * 2 * np.sqrt(vals)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.0, 4.3))
gs = GridSpec(2, 2, width_ratios=[4, 1.15], height_ratios=[1.15, 4], wspace=0.05, hspace=0.05)
axm = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0])
axt = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0], sharex=axm)
axrt = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1], sharey=axm)
axm.scatter(xx, yy, s=9, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
axm.add_patch(Ellipse([xx.mean(), yy.mean()], ew, eh, angle=ang, fc="none", ec=CRASH, lw=2.4))
axm.scatter([xx.mean()], [yy.mean()], s=55, c=CRASH, zorder=6)
axm.text(0.03, 0.92, "JOINT  p(x, y)", transform=axm.transAxes, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
axm.text(0.03, 0.04, "mean + covariance", transform=axm.transAxes, fontsize=10.5, color=CRASH)
axm.set_xlabel("X"); axm.set_ylabel("Y"); axm.set_xticks([]); axm.set_yticks([]); despine(axm)
axt.hist(xx, bins=30, color=WARM, alpha=0.78); axt.set_ylabel("p(x)", fontsize=11, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center")
axrt.hist(yy, bins=30, orientation="horizontal", color=WARM, alpha=0.78); axrt.set_xlabel("p(y)", fontsize=11)
for a in (axt, axrt):
    a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    for sp in a.spines.values():
        sp.set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

**Covariance** (the ellipse) is the 2-D 2nd moment — Pearson, rescaled. But
dependence lives in the **joint**; the marginals alone can't see it.

---

## Road 2 · Through the Density {.center}

Now the question is concrete: how far does the **joint** sit from the
**independent** version — the product of its marginals $p(x)\,p(y)$? Measure that
gap, in **bits**.

. . .

**Assume** the density's shape (parametric — fast, wrong in the tails) or **learn**
it (Gaussianization).

. . .

**Independence → entropy → MI → total correlation → Linfoot → Gaussianization**

---

## Independence as the Reference

Independent means $p(x, y) = p(x)\,p(y)$.  Shuffle one column and you *build* that
reference: same marginals, all dependence destroyed.  **Dependence = distance from
the shuffled version.**

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 450
x = rng.normal(size=n); y = 0.9 * x + 0.45 * rng.normal(size=n)
y_ref = rng.permutation(y)                      # same values, link destroyed
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 3.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
axL.scatter(x, y, s=20, c=WARM, alpha=0.55, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title("The data — dependent", fontsize=14)
axR.scatter(x, y_ref, s=20, c=COOL, alpha=0.55, edgecolors="none")
axR.set_title("Independent reference — Y shuffled", fontsize=14)
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xlabel("X"); ax.set_ylabel("Y"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

---

## Information & Entropy — the Intuition

Before any formula, two ideas:

- **Information = surprise** — a rare outcome tells you a lot; a near-certain one, almost nothing.
- **Entropy = average surprise** — how unpredictable a variable is.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.9
from scipy.stats import norm as _N
gx = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400)
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 2.9), sharey=True)
axL.fill_between(gx, _N.pdf(gx, 0, 0.5), color=COOL, alpha=0.4)
axL.plot(gx, _N.pdf(gx, 0, 0.5), color=INK, lw=2)
axL.set_title("peaked → predictable", fontsize=13)
axL.text(0.5, 0.55, "little surprise", transform=axL.transAxes, ha="center",
         fontsize=12, color=CRASH, fontweight="bold")
axR.fill_between(gx, _N.pdf(gx, 0, 2.3), color=WARM, alpha=0.4)
axR.plot(gx, _N.pdf(gx, 0, 2.3), color=INK, lw=2)
axR.set_title("spread → uncertain", fontsize=13)
axR.text(0.5, 0.55, "lots of surprise", transform=axR.transAxes, ha="center",
         fontsize=12, color=CRASH, fontweight="bold")
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("outcome"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

A peaked density is predictable (low entropy); a spread one keeps you guessing
(high). The next slides put **numbers** on this.

---

## #5 Entropy — Information Is Surprise

A rare event is **surprising**; a near-certain one tells you almost nothing:

$$I(x) = \log\frac{1}{p(x)}$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
p = np.linspace(0.004, 1.0, 500)
info = np.log2(1.0 / p)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.6))
ax.plot(p, info, color=COOL, lw=3)
for pv, lab, off in [(0.5, "ordinary day\n1 bit", (30, 10)),
                     (0.01, "crash day\n6.6 bits", (40, -8))]:
    ax.scatter([pv], [np.log2(1 / pv)], s=80, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(lab, (pv, np.log2(1 / pv)), textcoords="offset points", xytext=off,
                ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("P(event)"); ax.set_ylabel("surprise  (bits)")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The rarer the outcome, the more **bits** it carries.

---

## #5 Entropy — The Average Surprise

**Entropy is the *expected* surprise** — how unpredictable a variable is on
average. Volatile returns = high entropy = genuinely harder to predict.

$$H(X) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\frac{1}{p(X)}\right] = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
p = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 400)
H = -p * np.log2(p) - (1 - p) * np.log2(1 - p)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.9))
ax.plot(p, H, color=COOL, lw=3)
marks = [(0.5, "fair coin\n1 bit", (0, -52)), (0.9, "biased 90/10\n0.47 bit", (-2, 14))]
for pv, lab, off in marks:
    hv = -pv * np.log2(pv) - (1 - pv) * np.log2(1 - pv)
    ax.scatter([pv], [hv], s=80, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(lab, (pv, hv), textcoords="offset points", xytext=off,
                ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("P(heads)"); ax.set_ylabel("entropy H  (bits)")
ax.set_title("A fair coin is the hardest to predict", fontsize=13)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.15); despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

---

## #5 Entropy — In Pictures

Same question every morning: *what will today's return be?*

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
nE = 6000
bins = np.linspace(-8, 8, 33)


def hist_entropy_bits(s):
    cnt, _ = np.histogram(s, bins=bins)
    prob = cnt / cnt.sum()
    prob = prob[prob > 0]
    return -(prob * np.log2(prob)).sum() + 0.0  # +0.0 avoids displaying "-0.0"


panels = [("Pegged currency", 0.25 + 0.02 * rng.normal(size=nE), COOL),
          ("Calm asset", 0.6 * rng.normal(size=nE), COOL),
          ("Volatile asset", 2.5 * rng.normal(size=nE), WARM)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.4), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, s, col) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.hist(s, bins=bins, density=True, color=col, alpha=0.75)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=13)
    ax.text(0.5, 0.78, f"H = {hist_entropy_bits(s):.1f} bits", transform=ax.transAxes,
            ha="center", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold", color=INK,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc=PANEL, ec=GRID))
    ax.set_xlabel("daily return")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The wider the distribution, the more average surprise — the more **bits** it takes
to describe a day.

---

## KL Divergence — the Gap Between Densities

Entropy scored *one* density. **KL divergence** scores the gap between *two* — the
bits wasted using model $q$ when the truth is $p$ (zero only when they match):

$$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\,\|\,q)=\mathbb{E}_p\!\left[\log\frac{p}{q}\right]\;\ge\;0$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 2.4
from scipy.stats import norm as _Nk
xs = np.linspace(-5, 6.5, 400)
pp = _Nk.pdf(xs, 0.0, 1.0)                 # truth p
qq = _Nk.pdf(xs, 1.3, 1.7)                 # wrong model q
kl = float(np.sum(pp * np.log2(pp / qq)) * (xs[1] - xs[0]))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 2.4))
ax.fill_between(xs, pp, color=COOL, alpha=0.35)
ax.plot(xs, pp, color=INK, lw=2.2, label="p — truth")
ax.plot(xs, qq, color=WARM, lw=2.4, label="q — model")
ax.set_title(f"D_KL(p ‖ q) = {kl:.2f} bits", fontsize=13)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("outcome")
ax.legend(fontsize=12, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

Dependence is just KL **from independence**:
$I(X;Y)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{x,y}\,\|\,p_x\,p_y)$ — and total correlation is the same
for a whole vector. (Last slide's *shuffle* built exactly that reference.)

---

## #6 Mutual Information — In Pictures

Two variables can **share** surprise.  Toy data, the Venn it maps to, and the bits it earns:

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 2500
xd = rng.uniform(-2.5, 2.5, n); yd = xd**2 + 0.5 * rng.normal(size=n)  # dependent (curved)
xi = rng.normal(size=n); yi = rng.normal(size=n)                        # independent

def mi_bits(x, y):
    return mutual_information_bits(np.histogram2d(x, y, bins=10)[0])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.5, 6.0))
gs = GridSpec(2, 2, height_ratios=[1.25, 1], hspace=0.3, wspace=0.18)

# top row — the toy data
axDs = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
axDs.scatter(xd, yd, s=8, c=WARM, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
axDs.set_title("Dependent data (curved)", fontsize=13)
axIs = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1])
axIs.scatter(xi, yi, s=8, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
axIs.set_title("Independent data", fontsize=13)
for ax in (axDs, axIs):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)

# bottom row — the Venn it maps to, with MI
def mini_venn(ax, overlap, mi, label):
    ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 6); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    dx = 1.5 if overlap else 2.7
    _venn_circle(ax, (5 - dx, 3), 2.0, COOL)
    _venn_circle(ax, (5 + dx, 3), 2.0, WARM)
    if overlap:
        ax.text(5, 3, "MI", family="monospace", ha="center", va="center",
                fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=INK, zorder=6)
    ax.set_title(f"{label}  →  MI = {mi:.2f} bit", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")

mini_venn(fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0]), True, mi_bits(xd, yd), "overlap")
mini_venn(fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1]), False, mi_bits(xi, yi), "no overlap")
plt.show()
```

---

## #6 Mutual Information — The Honest Measure {.center}

**Shared information = each variable's surprise, minus the surprise of the pair:**

$$I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) \geq 0$$

**Equivalently — the distance from the independent reference:**

$$I(X;Y) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p(x,y)\,\|\,p(x)\,p(y)\big)$$

Zero *only* under independence; positive whenever they share structure.

---

## #6 Mutual Information — The Venn

```{python}
#| echo: false
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.2, 4.6))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 8); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_aspect("equal")
r, cx1, cx2, cy = 2.1, 4.0, 6.0, 4.2
_venn_circle(ax, (cx1, cy), r, COOL)
_venn_circle(ax, (cx2, cy), r, WARM)
ax.text(cx1 - 1.1, cy + 1.1, "H(X)", family="monospace", fontsize=20, color=COOL, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
ax.text(cx2 + 1.1, cy + 1.1, "H(Y)", family="monospace", fontsize=20, color=WARM, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
ax.text(5.0, cy, "I(X;Y)", family="monospace", fontsize=17, color=INK, fontweight="bold", ha="center", zorder=5)
ax.text(5.0, 0.8, "I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y)", family="monospace", fontsize=16, color=INK, ha="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc=PANEL, ec=GRID))
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The shared area is *what knowing one tells you about the other*.

---

## The Dial · One Value: $H(X)$

So far one sample = one **day** of one series: a single value.  Its uncertainty is **entropy**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# series + a reusable one-row panel (reused on the next two slides)
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
T = 26; t = np.arange(T)
common = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 1, T))
x_series = 0.7 * common + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.5, T))
y_series = 0.7 * np.roll(common, 1) + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.5, T))
x_series = (x_series - x_series.mean()) / x_series.std()
y_series = (y_series - y_series.mean()) / y_series.std()


def _dial(highlight=None, second_hl=None, measure="", desc="", mcolor=COOL, two=False):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 3.3))
    gs = GridSpec(1, 2, figure=fig, width_ratios=[1.85, 1], wspace=0.12)
    ax = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    ax.plot(t, x_series, color=COOL, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=4, label="X")
    if two:
        ax.plot(t, y_series, color=WARM, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=4, label="Y")
        ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=12, frameon=False, ncol=2)
    y0, y1 = ax.get_ylim()
    if highlight is not None:
        s, w = highlight
        ax.axvspan(s - 0.4, s + w - 0.6, color=COOL, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((s - 0.4, y0), w - 0.2, y1 - y0, boxstyle="round,pad=0",
                                    fill=False, edgecolor=COOL, lw=2.5, zorder=5))
    if second_hl is not None:
        s, w = second_hl
        ax.axvspan(s - 0.4, s + w - 0.6, color=WARM, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((s - 0.4, y0), w - 0.2, y1 - y0, boxstyle="round,pad=0",
                                    fill=False, edgecolor=WARM, lw=2.5, zorder=5))
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_xlabel("time (trading days) →", fontsize=13, color="#555")
    ax.set_ylabel("return", fontsize=13, color="#555")
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_edgecolor(GRID)
    axR = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 1]); axR.axis("off")
    axR.text(0.5, 0.66, desc, ha="center", fontsize=14, color="#555")
    axR.text(0.5, 0.28, measure, family="monospace", ha="center", fontsize=26,
             fontweight="bold", color=mcolor, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc=PANEL, ec=GRID))
    plt.show()


_dial(highlight=(8, 1), measure="H(X)", desc="uncertainty of one value")
```

One value per day → $H(X)$, the surprise of a single variable.

---

## The Dial · Two Values: $I(X;Y)$

Bring in the second series — same day, two values.  What does one tell you about the other?

```{python}
#| echo: false
_dial(highlight=(9, 1), measure="I(X;Y)", desc="shared info, one day",
      mcolor="#7d6b8f", two=True)
```

Shared surprise between two single values → $I(X;Y)$, mutual information.

---

## Going Multidimensional

Each sample is now a **vector**, not a number — covariance becomes a **matrix**:

$$\sigma_{xy}=\operatorname{cov}(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}\qquad\longrightarrow\qquad\Sigma_{xy}=\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.6
#| fig-height: 2.3
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 300
gT = rng.normal(0, 1, n)                                       # latent tech factor
gB = 0.6 * gT + np.sqrt(1 - 0.36) * rng.normal(0, 1, n)        # bank factor — sectors co-move
LX = rng.uniform(0.4, 1.1, 5); LY = rng.uniform(0.4, 1.1, 5)   # per-name factor loadings
eX = rng.uniform(0.4, 0.9, 5); eY = rng.uniform(0.4, 0.9, 5)   # per-name idiosyncratic noise
Xb = gT[:, None] * LX + eX * rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 5))          # 5 tech names   (n × 5)
Yb = gB[:, None] * LY + eY * rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 5))          # 5 bank names   (n × 5)
C = np.array([[pearsonr(Xb[:, i], Yb[:, j])[0] for j in range(5)] for i in range(5)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 2.3))
ax.imshow(C, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1, aspect="auto")   # wide cells so values don't crowd
for i in range(5):
    for j in range(5):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{C[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11,
                color="white" if abs(C[i, j]) > 0.55 else INK)
ax.set_xticks(range(5)); ax.set_yticks(range(5))
ax.set_xticklabels([f"B{j+1}" for j in range(5)], fontsize=10)
ax.set_yticklabels([f"T{i+1}" for i in range(5)], fontsize=10)
ax.set_title("5 tech × 5 banks = 25 correlations — which is THE one?", fontsize=11)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

One honest number from the whole matrix — same `corr(transform)` template.

---

## Pearson, Generalized — the RV Coefficient

One number from that whole matrix — the **same template**, a linear-kernel transform:

$$\mathrm{RV}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\frac{\langle\,\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top,\ \mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^\top\,\rangle_F}{\lVert\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^\top\rVert_F\;\lVert\mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^\top\rVert_F}\in[0,1]$$

```
CKA = corr( kernel(x) , kernel(y) )    ·  any kernel
RV  = corr(   x xᵀ    ,   y yᵀ    )    ·  linear kernel
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.3
rv = cka_linear(Xb, Yb)                                       # one score for the two baskets
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(5)
r2s, lcka = [], []
for _ in range(14):                                           # 1-D check: linear CKA == r²
    rho = rng2.uniform(-0.95, 0.95)
    z = rng2.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, rho], [rho, 1]], 200)
    r2s.append(pearsonr(z[:, 0], z[:, 1])[0] ** 2)
    lcka.append(cka_linear(z[:, 0], z[:, 1]))
fig, (axg, axc) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 2.3), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.5, 1]})
axg.barh([0], [1], color=PANEL, height=0.5, zorder=0)
axg.barh([0], [rv], color=COOL, height=0.5, zorder=1)
axg.set_xlim(0, 1); axg.set_ylim(-0.5, 0.5); axg.set_yticks([]); axg.set_xticks([0, 0.5, 1])
axg.text(rv + 0.02, 0, f"RV = {rv:.2f}", va="center", fontsize=15, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
axg.set_title("tech basket  ↔  bank basket  (one score)", fontsize=13); despine(axg)
axc.scatter(r2s, lcka, s=30, c=CRASH, alpha=0.85, edgecolors="none")
axc.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=GRID, lw=1.3, ls="--")
axc.set_xlim(0, 1); axc.set_ylim(0, 1)
axc.set_xlabel("Pearson²", fontsize=11); axc.set_ylabel("linear CKA", fontsize=11)
axc.set_title("1-D: RV = r²", fontsize=12); despine(axc)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

So **RV = CKA with a linear kernel** — the rung we already built. dCor, kernel-CKA
and MI were vector-native from birth; only **Pearson** & **Spearman** needed lifting.

---

## Entropy Goes Multidimensional — the Catch

RV needed no density. The **information road** does — a vector's entropy is built
from its whole **joint density** $p(\mathbf{x})$:

$$H(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\log\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{x})}\right],\qquad \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 2.4
bins = 8
N = 1000                                          # ≈ 4 years of trading days
d = np.arange(1, 8)
per_cell = N / np.power(float(bins), d)           # samples landing in each histogram cell
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 2.4))
ax.semilogy(d, per_cell, "-o", color=COOL, lw=2.6, ms=7)
ax.axhline(10, color=CRASH, ls="--", lw=1.6)
ax.text(7, 16, "need ≳ 10 per cell", color=CRASH, ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=12)
ax.annotate("d = 2: ok", (2, per_cell[1]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(10, 6),
            fontsize=12, color=INK)
ax.annotate("d ≥ 4: cells empty", (4, per_cell[3]), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(8, -2), fontsize=12, color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("dimension d   (8 bins / axis,  N = 1000 days)")
ax.set_ylabel("samples / cell")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

You can't histogram a 10-D density — the **curse of dimensionality**. The escape:
**Gaussianize** (entropy gets a closed form) or bound it with a surrogate (CKA, dCor).

---

## Total Correlation — MI for a Vector

Just as Pearson became RV, **mutual information becomes total correlation** — the
redundancy shared across *all* $d$ parts of a vector:

$$\mathrm{TC}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i H(X_i) - H(\mathbf{x}) \;\ge\; 0$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.6
#| fig-height: 2.4
rho = np.linspace(0, 0.95, 200)
tc2 = -0.5 * np.log2(1 - rho**2)                   # two Gaussians: total correlation == MI
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 2.4))
ax.plot(rho, tc2, color=COOL, lw=3)
ax.scatter([0.6], [-0.5 * np.log2(1 - 0.36)], s=80, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
ax.annotate("ρ = 0.6  →  0.32 bits", xy=(0.6, -0.5 * np.log2(1 - 0.36)),
            xytext=(0.04, 1.5), fontsize=12, color=INK,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GRID, lw=1.2))
ax.set_xlabel("correlation ρ   (two variables)"); ax.set_ylabel("TC  (bits)")
ax.set_ylim(0, 2.0); despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

. . .

For two variables it **is** the mutual information $I(X;Y)$ you already met — zero
only when every part is independent. Next: see it on the **dial**.

---

Widen the box: a sample is now a **vector** of consecutive days.

```{python}
_dial(highlight=(8, 3), measure="T(x)", desc="redundancy WITHIN the window")
```

## A Portfolio Is Not Two Columns

Two columns was a toy. A real book is **dozens** of names — the pairs explode, and
pairwise still can't see a move shared by *three or more*.

```{python}
#| echo: false
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 3.5))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 6); ax.axis("off")
d = 8; cx, cy, Rr = 5.0, 3.1, 2.2
pts = [(cx + Rr * np.cos(2 * np.pi * k / d + np.pi / 2),
        cy + Rr * np.sin(2 * np.pi * k / d + np.pi / 2)) for k in range(d)]
for i in range(d):
    for j in range(i + 1, d):
        ax.plot([pts[i][0], pts[j][0]], [pts[i][1], pts[j][1]], color=GRID, lw=0.7, alpha=0.7, zorder=1)
for (x, y) in pts:
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.24, facecolor=COOL, edgecolor=INK, lw=1.3, zorder=3))
ax.text(cx, cy, f"{d * (d - 1) // 2}\npairs", fontsize=16, color=CRASH, fontweight="bold",
        ha="center", va="center", zorder=5, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc="white", ec=CRASH))
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

One number for the whole book — **total correlation** — beats $\binom{d}{2}$ blind pairwise checks.

## A Real Book — Fifty Series at Once

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.7
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
T, M = 200, 48
common = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 1, T))            # one market factor everyone loads on
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.6, 3.7))
for m in range(M):
    s = rng.uniform(0.3, 1.0) * common + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.7, T))
    s = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
    ax.plot(s, color=COOL, alpha=0.16, lw=0.9)
for c, ld, sd in [(CRASH, 0.95, 1), (WARM, 0.6, 2), (INK, 0.35, 3)]:   # a few highlighted names
    rg = np.random.default_rng(sd)
    s = ld * common + np.cumsum(rg.normal(0, 0.7, T))
    s = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
    ax.plot(s, color=c, lw=2.2)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("time (trading days) →"); ax.set_ylabel("standardized return")
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

48 names, one hidden factor. Pearson reads **one pair**; total correlation reads the
whole grid at once — and its joint density is the one you *can't* histogram.

---

## The Shared Core — Total Correlation

Sum each name's surprise, subtract the joint's — the **overlap** is the redundancy
binding a basket ($\mathrm{TC}\ge0$; exactly $I(X;Y)$ at $d{=}2$). For a Gaussian it
comes **free** — no density to estimate:

$$\mathrm{TC}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i H(X_i) - H(\mathbf{x}) = -\tfrac12\log_2\det\mathbf{R}$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.8
#| fig-height: 2.7
R3 = np.full((3, 3), 0.6); np.fill_diagonal(R3, 1.0)          # 3 names, equicorrelated
tc_ex = -0.5 * np.log2(np.linalg.det(R3))                     # Gaussian total correlation, bits
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 2.7))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10); ax.set_ylim(0, 8.6); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_aspect("equal")
cols = [COOL, WARM, plotting.PALETTE["green"]]; names = ["X1", "X2", "X3"]
cx, cy, R, r = 5.0, 4.9, 1.15, 2.0
for k in range(3):
    ang = np.pi / 2 + k * 2 * np.pi / 3
    _venn_circle(ax, (cx + R * np.cos(ang), cy + R * np.sin(ang)), r, cols[k], alpha=0.30)
for (lx, ly), nm, col in zip([(cx, cy + R + r + 0.5), (cx - (R + r) * 0.92, cy - R * 0.5 - 0.2),
                              (cx + (R + r) * 0.92, cy - R * 0.5 - 0.2)], names, cols):
    ax.text(lx, ly, f"H({nm})", family="monospace", fontsize=15, color=col, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center")
ax.text(cx, cy, "TC", family="monospace", fontsize=20, color=INK, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center", zorder=8)
ax.text(cx, 0.7, f"3 names at ρ = 0.6   ⇒   TC = {tc_ex:.2f} bits   "
        f"(independent → 0)", family="monospace", fontsize=13, color=INK, ha="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc=PANEL, ec=GRID))
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Mutual Information *Between* Whole Groups

```{python}
#| echo: false
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.4, 5.0))
ax.set_xlim(0, 11); ax.set_ylim(0, 7.2); ax.axis("off"); ax.set_aspect("equal")

def _block(center, tagcol):
    bx, by = center
    for k in range(3):
        ang = np.pi / 2 + k * 2 * np.pi / 3
        pos = (bx + 0.55 * np.cos(ang), by + 0.55 * np.sin(ang))
        ax.add_patch(Circle(pos, 1.05, facecolor=tagcol, edgecolor=tagcol, lw=1.8, alpha=0.22, zorder=2))
        ax.add_patch(Circle(pos, 1.05, facecolor="none", edgecolor=tagcol, lw=1.8, alpha=0.6, zorder=3))
    ax.text(bx, by, "T", family="monospace", fontsize=16, color=tagcol, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center", zorder=6)

_block((3.2, 3.9), COOL); _block((7.8, 3.9), WARM)
ax.add_patch(Circle((5.5, 3.9), 1.35, facecolor="#7d6b8f", edgecolor="#5e4f6e", lw=1.6, alpha=0.30, zorder=4))
ax.text(5.5, 3.9, "I(X;Y)", family="monospace", fontsize=15, color=INK, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center", zorder=7)
ax.text(3.2, 6.1, "X = (X1..Xp)", family="monospace", fontsize=15, color=COOL, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
ax.text(7.8, 6.1, "Y = (Y1..Yq)", family="monospace", fontsize=15, color=WARM, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Each block has internal redundancy $T$; the lens between them is $I(X;Y)$ — and shrinking it is exactly Lecture 2.

---

## All the Measures — One Grid

Two knobs index every measure: **window width**, and **within vs between**.

|  | **WITHIN** one variable | **BETWEEN** two variables |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **one value** | $H(X)$ — entropy | $I(X;Y)$ — mutual information |
| **a window** | $T(\mathbf{x})$ — total correlation | $I(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{y})$ — mutual information |

One family — the dial picks which.

---

## #7 Linfoot R — MI on the Correlation Scale

$$R = \sqrt{1 - e^{-2\,I}} \in [0, 1]$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=2000)
mi_banks = mutual_information_xy(a, b) / np.log(2)
R_banks = linfoot_r(mi_banks * np.log(2))
mi_axis = np.linspace(0, 3, 300)
R_curve = np.sqrt(1 - np.exp(-2 * mi_axis * np.log(2)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 2.7))
ax.plot(mi_axis, R_curve, color=COOL, lw=3)
ax.scatter([mi_banks], [R_banks], s=90, c=CRASH, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(f"the banks: {mi_banks:.1f} bits  →  R = {R_banks:.2f}",
            (mi_banks, R_banks), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(20, -16),
            fontsize=13, color=INK)
ax.set_xlabel("mutual information  (bits)"); ax.set_ylabel("Linfoot R")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05); despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Bits map onto the familiar $[0, 1]$ axis — and for a Gaussian pair, $R = |\rho|$ **exactly**.

---

## It All Comes Back to $p(\mathbf{x})$

Every Road-2 measure is the **same integral** — an average over the density. Each is
helpless without $p(\mathbf{x})$:

$$H(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; -\int p(\mathbf{x})\,\log p(\mathbf{x})\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}$$

$$I(X;Y) \;=\; \int p(\mathbf{x})\,\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{p(x)\,p(y)}\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}$$

$$\mathrm{TC}(\mathbf{x}) \;=\; \int p(\mathbf{x})\,\log\frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{\prod_i p(x_i)}\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}$$

. . .

Road 1 dodged this with **distances and kernels**. Road 2 must face it head-on —
**estimate $p(\mathbf{x})$.** So how hard is that, dimension by dimension?

---

## Estimating $p(\mathbf{x})$ · One Dimension

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.3
from scipy.stats import norm as _Nd, skewnorm as _SN
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
easy = rng.normal(0, 1, 1500)                          # a clean bell
hard = _SN.rvs(6, size=1500, random_state=7)           # skewed, heavy on one side
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.3))
for ax, data, name in [(axes[0], easy, "easy — a bell"), (axes[1], hard, "hard — skewed")]:
    g = np.linspace(data.min() - 0.5, data.max() + 0.5, 300)
    ax.hist(data, bins=32, density=True, color="#c9cdd4", alpha=0.95,
            edgecolor="white", lw=0.6, label="histogram (data)")
    ax.plot(g, _Nd.pdf(g, data.mean(), data.std()), color=CRASH, lw=2.4, ls="--",
            label="parametric (Gaussian)")
    ax.plot(g, gaussian_kde(data)(g), color=COOL, lw=2.6, label="learned (KDE)")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=13); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=10.5, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Start from the **histogram** of the data, then **assume** a Gaussian *or* **learn** it
(KDE). The Gaussian nails the bell and misses the skew; the learned curve fits both.

---

## Estimating $p(\mathbf{x})$ · Two Dimensions

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=900)
u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=900)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
for ax, x, y, col, name in [(axes[0], a, b, COOL, "easy — a tilted blob"),
                            (axes[1], u, v, WARM, "hard — a V")]:
    X = np.column_stack([x, y])
    g = np.linspace(X.min() - 0.5, X.max() + 0.5, 130)
    XX, YY = np.meshgrid(g, g)
    Zg = multivariate_normal(X.mean(0), np.cov(X.T)).pdf(np.dstack([XX, YY]))          # parametric
    Zk = gaussian_kde(X.T)(np.vstack([XX.ravel(), YY.ravel()])).reshape(XX.shape)      # learned
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=8, c=col, alpha=0.32, edgecolors="none")
    ax.contour(XX, YY, Zg, levels=5, colors=[CRASH], linewidths=1.1, linestyles="dashed")
    ax.contour(XX, YY, Zk, levels=5, colors=[INK], linewidths=1.1)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=13); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Dashed = a fitted **Gaussian** (whose only dependence is *correlation* — its shadow);
solid = the **learned** density. The Gaussian misses the V; the learned one wraps it.

---

## Estimating $p(\mathbf{x})$ · Many Dimensions

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 2.7
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.6, 2.7))
d1 = rng.normal(0, 1, 1200)                                   # 1-D: a histogram (as before)
g1 = np.linspace(-3.6, 3.6, 200)
axes[0].hist(d1, bins=28, density=True, color="#c9cdd4", alpha=0.95, edgecolor="white", lw=0.5)
axes[0].plot(g1, gaussian_kde(d1)(g1), color=COOL, lw=2.4)
axes[0].set_title("1-D · a histogram", fontsize=12)
p2 = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, 0.6], [0.6, 1]], 500)   # 2-D: a density (as before)
gg = np.linspace(-3.6, 3.6, 90); XX, YY = np.meshgrid(gg, gg)
Zk = gaussian_kde(p2.T)(np.vstack([XX.ravel(), YY.ravel()])).reshape(XX.shape)
axes[1].scatter(p2[:, 0], p2[:, 1], s=8, c=COOL, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
axes[1].contour(XX, YY, Zk, levels=5, colors=[INK], linewidths=1.0)
axes[1].set_title("2-D · a density", fontsize=12)
q = rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 2))                                # d-D: no picture
axes[2].scatter(q[:, 0], q[:, 1], s=8, c=GRID, alpha=0.18, edgecolors="none")
axes[2].text(0.5, 0.5, "?", transform=axes[2].transAxes, ha="center", va="center",
             fontsize=60, color=CRASH, fontweight="bold")
axes[2].set_title("d-D · no picture", fontsize=12, color=CRASH)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp in ax.spines.values():
        sp.set_edgecolor(GRID)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A histogram works in 1-D, a density in 2-D — but past 3-D there's no picture, and a
histogram needs $\sim\!10^{d}$ samples. The only survivor is to **learn** the density.

---

## Two Ways to Get $p(\mathbf{x})$: Assume It, or Learn It

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Assume a family** — *parametric*

- pick a shape: Gaussian, $t$, mixture
- cheap, little data, scales to high-$d$
- but **rigid** — a Gaussian's only dependence is **correlation**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Learn the shape** — *nonparametric*

- let the data carve the density
- flexible — Vs, fat tails, modes
- KDE in low-$d$; high-$d$ needs an **invertible learned map**
:::
::::

. . .

Gaussianization takes the best of both: **learn** an invertible map that turns the
data *into* a Gaussian — flexible shape, exact likelihoods. *(Next.)*

---

## #8 Gaussianization — Fit the V Three Ways

Fit a **Gaussian**, a **Student-$t$**, and **RBIG** to the V; contours are each
model's joint density, with its score on the right.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.1
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import rbig
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from scipy.stats import multivariate_t as _mvt
u61, v61 = datasets.convex_payoff(n=1200, seed=0)
X61 = np.column_stack([u61, v61]).astype(float)
loc61, cov61 = X61.mean(0), np.cov(X61.T)
gN = multivariate_normal(loc61, cov61)
dfg = max(((d, _mvt(loc61, cov61 * (d - 2) / d, df=d).logpdf(X61).mean()) for d in (3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 15)),
          key=lambda z: z[1])[0]
tN = _mvt(loc61, cov61 * (dfg - 2) / dfg, df=dfg)
mR = rbig.AnnealedRBIG(random_state=0); mR.fit(X61)


def _hmi(s):
    return mutual_information_xy(s[:, 0], s[:, 1]) / np.log(2)


gsamp = gN.rvs(7000, random_state=1); tsamp = tN.rvs(7000, random_state=1)
rsamp = np.asarray(mR.sample(7000, random_state=1))
gll = gN.logpdf(X61).mean(); tll = tN.logpdf(X61).mean(); rll = -rbig.negative_log_likelihood(mR, X61)
mis = [_hmi(gsamp), _hmi(tsamp), _hmi(rsamp)]
trueMI = _hmi(X61)
gx = np.linspace(X61[:, 0].min() - 1, X61[:, 0].max() + 1, 110)
gy = np.linspace(X61[:, 1].min() - 1, X61[:, 1].max() + 1, 110)
GX, GY = np.meshgrid(gx, gy)
Zg = gN.pdf(np.dstack([GX, GY])); Zt = tN.pdf(np.dstack([GX, GY]))
Zr = gaussian_kde(rsamp[:2500].T)(np.vstack([GX.ravel(), GY.ravel()])).reshape(GX.shape)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 4.1))
gsp = GridSpec(2, 3, width_ratios=[4, 1.1, 2.5], height_ratios=[1, 4], wspace=0.05, hspace=0.05)
axT = fig.add_subplot(gsp[0, 0]); axMn = fig.add_subplot(gsp[1, 0]); axRt = fig.add_subplot(gsp[1, 1])
axSt = fig.add_subplot(gsp[:, 2]); axSt.axis("off")
axMn.scatter(X61[:, 0], X61[:, 1], s=7, c=GRID, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none")
axMn.contour(GX, GY, Zg, levels=5, colors=[CRASH], linewidths=1.2, linestyles="dashed")
axMn.contour(GX, GY, Zt, levels=5, colors=[WARM], linewidths=1.1, linestyles="dotted")
axMn.contour(GX, GY, Zr, levels=5, colors=[COOL], linewidths=1.5)
axMn.set_xticks([]); axMn.set_yticks([]); despine(axMn)
axMn.legend(handles=[Line2D([0], [0], color=COOL, lw=1.6, label="RBIG"),
                     Line2D([0], [0], color=WARM, lw=1.1, ls=":", label="Student-t"),
                     Line2D([0], [0], color=CRASH, lw=1.2, ls="--", label="Gaussian")],
            fontsize=10, frameon=False, loc="upper center", ncol=3, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.02))
axT.hist(X61[:, 0], bins=40, color="#c9cdd4", alpha=0.95, edgecolor="white", lw=0.4); axT.axis("off")
axRt.hist(X61[:, 1], bins=40, orientation="horizontal", color="#c9cdd4", alpha=0.95, edgecolor="white", lw=0.4)
axRt.axis("off")
axSt.text(0.0, 0.97, f"n = {len(X61)} samples", fontsize=12, color="#666", transform=axSt.transAxes)
for j, (nm, c, ll, mi) in enumerate([("RBIG (learned)", COOL, rll, mis[2]),
                                     ("Student-t", WARM, tll, mis[1]),
                                     ("Gaussian", CRASH, gll, mis[0])]):
    yb = 0.82 - j * 0.27
    axSt.text(0.0, yb, nm, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=c, transform=axSt.transAxes)
    axSt.text(0.06, yb - 0.085, f"log-lik  {ll:+.2f}", fontsize=12, color=INK, transform=axSt.transAxes)
    axSt.text(0.06, yb - 0.165, f"MI  {mi:.2f} bits", fontsize=12, color=INK, transform=axSt.transAxes)
axSt.text(0.0, 0.02, f"true MI = {trueMI:.2f} bits", fontsize=12, style="italic", color=INK, transform=axSt.transAxes)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Both ellipses sit blind over the bend; only the RBIG contour **wraps** the V.

---

## #8 Gaussianization — RBIG vs Parametric

The same three fits, scored head-to-head — RBIG wins the likelihood *and* recovers the bits:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.4
dll = [0.0, tll - gll, rll - gll]
labels = ["Gaussian", "Student-t", "RBIG"]; cols = [CRASH, WARM, COOL]
fig, (axL, axM) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
axL.bar(labels, dll, color=cols)
axL.set_title("log-likelihood gain over Gaussian", fontsize=12); axL.set_ylabel("nats / point")
for i, val in enumerate(dll):
    axL.text(i, val, f"+{val:.2f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11, color=INK)
axL.set_ylim(0, max(dll) * 1.25 + 0.05)
axM.bar(labels, mis, color=cols)
axM.axhline(trueMI, color=INK, ls="--", lw=1.3)
axM.text(2.4, trueMI + 0.03, "true MI", color=INK, fontsize=10, ha="right")
axM.set_title("mutual information recovered (bits)", fontsize=12)
for i, val in enumerate(mis):
    axM.text(i, val + 0.02, f"{val:.2f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11, color=INK)
axM.set_ylim(0, max(mis) * 1.3 + 0.1)
for ax in (axL, axM):
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=11); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The Gaussian and Student-$t$ are elliptical — blind to the bend. RBIG fits the V, so it
earns the **likelihood** and recovers the **bits** of dependence the others miss.

## The Synthesis — Two Roads, by Complexity

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.5))
ax.set_xlim(0, 11); ax.set_ylim(0, 6.6); ax.axis("off")


def _station(x, y, label, color, hi=False):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - 0.78, y - 0.32), 1.56, 0.64,
                                boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.14",
                                fc="white", ec=color, lw=2.8 if hi else 1.8, zorder=3))
    ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, color=color,
            fontweight="bold" if hi else "normal", zorder=4)


# decision node + branches
ax.text(0.55, 3.5, "need the\ndensity?", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.annotate("", xy=(1.7, 5.0), xytext=(0.95, 3.95), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=COOL, lw=2.2))
ax.annotate("", xy=(1.7, 2.0), xytext=(0.95, 3.05), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=WARM, lw=2.2))
ax.text(1.05, 4.55, "no", fontsize=11, color=COOL, style="italic")
ax.text(1.05, 2.4, "yes", fontsize=11, color=WARM, style="italic")
# Road 1 — a score, no density
ax.text(2.3, 5.95, "Road 1 · a score, no density", color=COOL, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
r1 = [("Pearson", 2.7), ("Spearman", 4.5), ("dist corr", 6.3), ("CKA", 8.1)]
for lab, x in r1:
    _station(x, 5.0, lab, COOL)
for (l1, x1), (l2, x2) in zip(r1, r1[1:]):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x2 - 0.82, 5.0), xytext=(x1 + 0.82, 5.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=GRID, lw=1.4))
# Road 2 — model the density
ax.text(2.3, 0.95, "Road 2 · model the density", color=WARM, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
r2 = [("Gaussian", 4.7, False), ("Student-t", 6.6, False), ("RBIG", 9.3, True)]
for lab, x, hi in r2:
    _station(x, 2.0, lab, CRASH if hi else WARM, hi=hi)
for (l1, x1, _a), (l2, x2, _b) in zip(r2, r2[1:]):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x2 - 0.82, 2.0), xytext=(x1 + 0.82, 2.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=GRID, lw=1.4))
ax.text(5.65, 2.72, "assume the shape", fontsize=10.5, color="#777", style="italic", ha="center")
ax.text(9.3, 2.72, "learn it", fontsize=10.5, color=CRASH, style="italic", ha="center")
# complexity axis
ax.annotate("", xy=(10.6, 0.25), xytext=(0.3, 0.25), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2.2))
ax.text(0.3, -0.05, "cheap · linear", fontsize=11, color="#555")
ax.text(10.6, -0.05, "costly · exact", fontsize=11, color="#555", ha="right")
ax.text(5.5, 0.42, "complexity →", fontsize=11.5, color=INK, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Detection is the easy part — most rungs past Pearson catch the V. The real trade-off is
**complexity**: a score is cheap; the full density costs more, but only it lets you
**sample, propagate, and price the tails**.

## Every Method, Both Characters

The full ladder plus MI through three densities — all on one $[0,1]$ scale
(MI shown as **Linfoot $R$**, so the bits sit next to the correlations):

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import rbig
from scipy.stats import multivariate_t as _mvt63


def char_scores(x, y):
    x = np.asarray(x, float); y = np.asarray(y, float); X = np.column_stack([x, y])
    loc, cov = X.mean(0), np.cov(X.T)
    g = multivariate_normal(loc, cov)
    df = max(((d, _mvt63(loc, cov * (d - 2) / d, df=d).logpdf(X).mean()) for d in (3, 4, 5, 7, 10, 15)),
             key=lambda z: z[1])[0]
    t = _mvt63(loc, cov * (df - 2) / df, df=df)
    m = rbig.AnnealedRBIG(random_state=0); m.fit(X)
    miR = lambda s: linfoot_r(mutual_information_xy(s[:, 0], s[:, 1]))   # nats → Linfoot R ∈ [0,1]
    return [abs(pearsonr(x, y)[0]), abs(spearmanr(x, y)[0]), distance_correlation(x, y), cka_rbf(x, y),
            miR(g.rvs(8000, random_state=1)), miR(t.rvs(8000, random_state=1)),
            miR(np.asarray(m.sample(8000, random_state=1)))]


a, b, _ = datasets.two_banks(n=1000)
u, v = datasets.convex_payoff(n=1000)
banks, convex = char_scores(a, b), char_scores(u, v)
methods = ["Pearson", "Spearman", "dist\ncorr", "CKA", "MI·\nGauss", "MI·\nt", "MI·\nRBIG"]
xs = np.arange(7); wbar = 0.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11.5, 4.5))
ax.axvspan(-0.5, 1.5, color=CRASH, alpha=0.05)
ax.axvline(3.5, color=GRID, lw=1.6, ls="--")
ax.bar(xs - wbar / 2, banks, wbar, color=COOL, label="Banks (a line)")
ax.bar(xs + wbar / 2, convex, wbar, color=WARM, label="Convex (a V)")
ax.text(1.5, 1.0, "Road 1 · a score", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(5.0, 1.0, "Road 2 · MI via a density", ha="center", fontsize=12, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(0.5, 0.14, "linear:\nblind to the V", ha="center", fontsize=10.5, color=CRASH,
        style="italic", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xticks(xs); ax.set_xticklabels(methods, fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel("dependence detected  (0–1)"); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.1)
ax.legend(fontsize=12, frameon=False, ncol=2, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.03))
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

On the **Banks** everything agrees. On the **V**, the linear rungs *and* the parametric
MIs (Gaussian, $t$) stay flat — only **dist corr, CKA, and MI·RBIG** catch the bend.

---

## Which Road, When?

They **agree on detection** — but hand you different things.

| | **Kernel score** · HSIC, dCor, CKA | **Gaussianization** · RBIG, flows |
|---|---|---|
| Gives you | a number: *how much* | the whole density / map |
| Units | kernel-dependent score | **bits** (+ Linfoot R) |
| Cost & data | cheap, one-shot | iterative, data-hungry |
| Invertible? | no | **yes** → generate, propagate |

---

## Which Road, When? {.center}

The **shortcut** (a score) answers *is there dependence?*

. . .

The **exact map** (a density) lets you *use* it — generate, propagate,
neutralize.

---

## The Punchline → Lab {.center}

The same ladder, now on **real S&P 500 returns**.

. . .

JPMorgan & Bank of America share ~0.7 bits of information.

They fall into their worst days together **~7× more often** than
independence allows.

. . .

*That is the dependence correlation cannot see — and the one that actually
threatens a portfolio.*
